title: Presenting Symptoms
subject: Pathology
summary: Clinicians learn to interpret the first clues a patient gives. By linking history, exam and local disease patterns, they build a differential, order the right tests and act before complications arise.

sections.p: Presenting symptoms are the first complaints that bring a patient to care. They are the gateway to diagnosis and management, especially in low‑resource settings where investigations may be limited.
b: They are subjective reports of pain, discomfort or functional loss.
They guide the initial clinical reasoning and triage.

sections.p: Severity is gauged by the impact on daily life and the urgency of intervention. Staging is disease‑specific; for example, fever severity is judged by temperature and associated signs.
b: Mild: <38.5°C, no systemic signs.
Moderate: 38.5–39.5°C, possible dehydration.
Severe: >39.5°C, altered mental status or shock.

sections.p: In East Africa, common causes of presenting symptoms are infectious, nutritional, and environmental. Prioritise the most prevalent local diseases.
b: Fever – malaria, typhoid, dengue, bacterial sepsis, HIV flare.
Abdominal pain – amoebic dysentery, typhoid, appendicitis, malaria.
Chest pain – pneumonia, tuberculosis, malaria, cardiac ischemia.

sections.p: Symptoms are often vague; the clinician must elicit details and look for red flags. Contextual clues (season, travel, exposure) refine the differential.
b: Ask about onset, duration, character, relieving factors and associated symptoms.
Note systemic signs: pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, oedema.
Use simple bedside tests: pulse, BP, capillary refill, mental status.

sections.p: Investigation choice depends on availability and the likelihood of life‑threatening disease.

t.b: Is the patient febrile due to malaria? A positive result confirms malaria, guiding antimalarial therapy.

sections.p: Certain features mandate urgent action to prevent morbidity and mortality.
b: Altered consciousness, hypotension, severe chest pain, haemoptysis, massive bleeding, sudden severe headache, high fever with rigors, persistent vomiting or diarrhoea leading to dehydration.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Drug choice reflects efficacy, safety, and local resistance patterns.
b: Malaria – artemisinin‑based combination therapy; avoid quinine if renal impairment.
Severe bacterial infection – empirical broad‑spectrum antibiotics, adjust when cultures return.
Dehydration – oral rehydration solution or IV fluids if severe.
Pain – paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if bleeding risk or renal disease.

sections.p: Re‑assessment is critical; prevention focuses on vaccination, vector control, and patient education.
b: Repeat temperature and symptom review within 24–48h.
Encourage malaria prophylaxis, hand hygiene, safe food practices.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, pneumococcus, and influenza where available.

sections.p: Many local diseases mimic each other; recognising subtle differences avoids misdiagnosis.
b: Malaria vs. dengue – both cause fever; dengue has retro‑orbital pain and haemorrhagic signs.
Typhoid vs. dysentery – both abdominal pain; typhoid has rose spots, dysentery has bloody stools.

sections.p: Lab and clinical findings can be falsely normal or abnormal in resource‑limited settings.
b: Malaria smear may be negative in low parasitaemia; repeat or use RDT.
Leukopenia can be normal in malaria; look for thrombocytopenia.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dehydration with inability to take oral fluids
High fever with rigors or persistent after 48h

faq.q: What is the first thing to do when a patient presents with fever in a rural clinic?
faq.a: Take a focused history, perform a quick physical exam, and if malaria is likely, start empiric antimalarial while awaiting RDT or microscopy.

faq.q: How do you differentiate malaria from dengue when RDTs are unavailable?
faq.a: Look for retro‑orbital pain, rash, and haemorrhagic signs for dengue; malaria often has splenomegaly and cyclical fevers.

faq.q: Why is paracetamol preferred over NSAIDs for fever in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk and can worsen renal function; paracetamol is safer and effective for fever and pain.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with fever, headache, and a rash. What is the most likely diagnosis and first step? — Dengue fever; start IV fluids and monitor for haemorrhage.
A child has abdominal pain and fever. How would you rule out appendicitis versus typhoid? — Look for rebound tenderness, anorexia, and perform a Widal test; if uncertain, start empirical antibiotics.
A patient with chronic cough and weight loss is brought to the ward. What red flag would prompt immediate investigation? — Night sweats and haemoptysis suggest tuberculosis; start sputum microscopy.
You suspect malaria but the RDT is negative. What is your next move? — Repeat smear or use a second RDT; if still negative and fever persists, consider bacterial sepsis.
A patient with fever and jaundice is admitted. What is the differential and first investigation? — Hepatitis B, malaria, sepsis; check liver enzymes and malaria RDT.

A young adult presents with fever and a swollen neck. How do you differentiate meningitis from cervical lymphadenitis? — Look for neck stiffness, photophobia, and perform a lumbar puncture if meningitis is suspected.
A patient with fever and haemoptysis is stable. What is the next best investigation? — Chest X‑ray to assess for pulmonary infiltrates or TB.
A patient with fever and severe headache reports pain behind the eyes. What is the most likely cause and treatment? — Dengue; supportive care with fluids and avoid NSAIDs.
